s12.slug: WEDNESDAY · 3:10 PM · DUPRE STREET, THE FRONT STEPS — THE MOON

body.text: He comes home from Banks Street a little after three with the Gulf in his clothes. Tony kept him on to hose the floor down to the drain and stack the empty ice chests, MISS ODILE on top, and his hands are red to the wrists from the ice, the knuckles shiny and stiff, so that he works the gate latch with the heel of one. Lena walked home ahead of him at two with her father’s second ring of keys, and with the carnations she bought out of the florist’s bucket by the door next to the market, at lunch, out of her own apron pocket.
body.else: He comes home from the Quarter a little after three on the bus up Esplanade, with powdered sugar worked into the front of the Carhartt that no amount of slapping at it on the bus has moved. He left Theo and Laney and the others at the river with a list that had sections. Lena got home from the register before him.

body: She’s on the porch swing in the Broussard’s Seafood sweatshirt with her boots up on the rail and her father’s keys in her fist, and her hair coming down out of its pencil. Beside her on the slats lies a small bunch of white carnations wrapped in the classifieds out of Monday’s paper. She watches him come up the walk. She doesn’t say what she’s out here for.

The afternoon is clear and hard and blue, the cold that came in behind the parade still sitting on the city. Dupre Street has gone back to work: a mail truck working its way down the block from the corner, two doors down a man up a ladder taking a Saints flag down off his gutter and folding it over his knee. Across the street the Odyssey sits at the curb under its dust with WHO DAT · 1 DAYS still on the back glass and Josie’s lipstick zero gone pink and smeary in two days of weather.

He sits down on the top step, and the RAZR goes against his ribs. The little window on the lid says SKYE (MISFIT). Behind him the swing stops. When he opens the phone and turns his head to get it to his ear, Lena is watching him do it.
“This is Burnaby,” Skye says. “Burnaby would like to know where you are.”
“On the front steps.”
“Whose front steps.”
“The man on the porch’s. In Mid-City.”
“Oh good. Stay there. I can picture that.” A generator hums under her, and somebody close by yells for a C-stand, and doesn’t get it, and yells again.

body.text: She doesn’t ask. She lets the man yell for his C-stand a third time and waits on the other end of it.
“I got it,” Jack says. The step is cold through his jeans. “Last night. I was by myself.” Up the street the mail truck stops and starts. “It was yours. I could tell.”
On her end a door shuts, and the lot is gone, and there’s only the generator through a wall.
“I’ve never sent anybody one I didn’t take *for* them,” Skye says.
Right behind it she laughs at herself, short, through her nose. “That’s a terrible thing to say on a lunch break. Forget I said it on a lunch break. Remember it some other time.”
“Did you get it?”
He tells her the truth, because it’s her asking. “I got it. I opened it. Then I erased it.”
On her end a door shuts, and the lot is gone, and there’s only the generator through a wall. The mail truck stops two houses up and the carrier gets out with a bundle.
“Okay,” Skye says. “That one was yours to erase.”

“So,” Skye says. “I read my two a.m. text. You deleted my best work unopened, in a Catholic grandmother’s attic. That’s the most respectful thing anyone’s ever done to me, and I want to file a complaint.”
“Take it up with the grandmother.”

“I bet she has a *form*. I bet it’s in French.” The C-stand man gives up. When she speaks again she has moved off somewhere, or put her back to a wall, and her voice is down close to the phone. “Was it the house, or was it you?”
Jack looks at the Odyssey across the street, the lipstick zero. Behind him one of the keys in Lena’s fist touches another.
“Both,” he says.
A gust comes up Dupre Street and turns the newspaper over on the carnations. In Burnaby a door shuts on the lot. “…Okay,” Skye says. “Both I can work with.”

body: “News from the North,” she says, back at full speed. “The torch came through today.”
“The Olympic one?”

“Is there a lesser torch? A man in a white tracksuit ran past craft services with fire, and everybody clapped like it was a person. Russ cried. Kyle tried to get a picture of it and got the back of a Mountie.” A plastic lid comes off something. “And we reshot Wade. The porch. The light was wrong on Monday, apparently, the light was *lying*, so we did it all again, and the beard did your pause, and I cried again.” The lid goes back on. “They came. That’s the worst part. They come when they’re called now.”
“That’s the job.”
“That’s the job,” she says, “and I hate how much I like it.” The yelling has started up again outside her door: a name that isn’t hers, then hers. “Quick. Did the man on the porch go back to work?”
“Seven this morning. God was willing. It was on the sign.”
“What happened to the sign?”

body.text: “He folded it in four and buttoned it in his shirt pocket.”
body.else: “I don’t know. I was in the Quarter, eating sugar.”

body.text: “Of course he did. That’s a man who keeps a sign. I knew that about him from Canada.”
body.else: “Find out. I need to know what happens to the sign. I’m invested in the sign.”

body.text: “Okay. I have to go be Cassie, and I’m on until they run out of dark. Remember the moon.”
body.else: “Okay. I have to go be Cassie, and I’m on until they run out of dark. New rule. If I text you the moon, it means I’m working all night and you’re not allowed to worry.”

body: Behind him the swing hasn’t moved. Lena has her boots crossed on the rail and the keys gone still in her hand, and she is looking across the street at the van.
“Tonight’s the moon,” Skye says.

journal.title: Skye Callender
journal.text: Skye Callender, two Ls. Wouldn’t give me a last name — said *Out* — till she texted it to me on the floor in Denver. Met her in a window seat in Montecito, reading O’Connor for a part and had the grandmother exactly backwards. Acts — since she was eleven. Starts here in January: spring, undeclared. She’s declared enough, she says. Doesn’t drink where there are phones. Drives a dented ’91 Saab she says is Swedish. It’s GM. Walked into the Pacific in November like it was a bath, and dared me in after her in my clothes. Asked to kiss me — out loud. She was the one who stopped, in the grandmother’s voice. Typed herself into my phone as SKYE (MISFIT), and called herself from it. Took ten hours to answer my correction. Work, she said — a carpet and a wall. Her car’s an orphan now, and it’s my fault. Nearly three hours at the Starlite, a truck stop up the 101, with Nonna’s pie on the table. Cast me as the Bible salesman. Wanted to know what believing is like — not what I believe. Wants me to miss her a reasonable amount. Get the window, she said. Kissed me again against the Saab in the lot. Slower. On purpose. She was the one who stopped — her thumb on my mouth. She’s on TV. *Sweetwater*, Thursdays at nine: she plays Cassidy, the nice one. Gina screamed. I explained GM to her. In her own car. Thanksgiving: texted me the whole drive from Pittsburgh. Spent it at her mother’s place in Studio City; the parrot says ‘momager.’ Told me not to watch her show. Wants me to be specific. We’re friends on Facebook now — one mutual friend: Theo, who knows everybody. Saturday night she called. Three hours on the porch. Made me do my family. Asked what Advent is. Asked if the TV part matters. Fell asleep in the middle of the Madonna. Monday she drove two hours from LA to sit in a car with me for two more, and set an alarm so she’d leave. Watched the President with the sound off and read his face like a script. Her phone learned a trick in September; she’s still not over it. Gives every truck on the 101 a whole life in three sentences. Knows every word of ‘Thunder Road.’ The tape deck finally let go of *Rumours*. Invited me to LA; I work Saturdays. Doesn’t take people home. Saturday, in daylight, on a rock above the tide pools: fractions, for the placement test. I drew her a pie. Sharks were a lie. I told her a saint broke in. Drove me to Burbank in the rain to be her cousin from Ohio. Everybody on a set wants something from her; she smiles for every phone. Plays a preacher’s daughter who forgives a thief. She played it dry. Washed a borrowed dress in a laundromat at one in the morning; it lived. Thinks the Immaculate Conception is the other one. Took the math test with forty kids and nobody looked at her once. Doesn’t take people home. Took me home. Lives on Del Playa, in a house with a darkroom she isn’t allowed in and two boards under the porch the boys won’t let on the rack — she’ll live there in January. On her bed I said no. She stopped everything and asked me why, and we talked till it got light. I told her it’s a no right now. She said she can work with that. Picked my present for the church party: a Magic 8-Ball. Every answer’s a line reading, she says. Her car died in Buellton; I pushed. She’s seen Our Lady of Guadalupe on every taco truck in the Valley and thought she was a brand. Friday night she took my ‘right now’ apart, point by point, with visual aids, and made a very good case. It’s still right now. I said no again, and she stopped right there and nowhere else. Came to the Anchor in my shirt; Gloria rated her boysenberry. She’s going to ask every day, she says. It’s in her calendar. Slept at her house. Just slept. She says that doesn’t happen. Taught me to surf at Ellery on Gaudete Sunday. I’m terrible. I go home in six days. She isn’t counting. Played Hale in her car from my description. Made me answer the question I couldn’t at the Starlite. Thursday at one in the morning, no moon at all, she drove the bluff with the lights off. Not before Christmas, she said — Christmas and New Year’s and long distance are too much for something new. When I get back we’re dating. Officially. A whole thing. She counted. GM is killing Saab. I’m on the hook. Christmas week: Theo’s known her since they were eleven — his father’s company makes her show. She calls him Ted; nobody else does. She saw us walk into the Hallorans’ together and hid behind a ficus. “Peace mission” was for him. He ran into her at a party in the hills on the twenty-second, and she says he knows. She had me do the weather barefoot in the snow. Seventeen days; she’s not counting. Christmas morning my family found her — Gina gave me her show on DVD. They know her as the nice one. She wants it on her headstone. The day after Christmas my whole family watched season two of her show. She was eighteen, in a blazer, on a dock. She’s good — Dad said so, and she says nobody says good. Nonna prays for Cassidy now. She bought Chesterton used on Ventura without knowing it was my book, and wants to know who picked midnight. The Monday after Christmas she called, and we talked till my phone died. New Year’s Eve she watched my ball drop on the East Coast feed at nine her time and texted, so she’d be at midnight with me. Then she had her own, at three in the morning mine, from a locked den in the hills. I told her I called Ted *Ted*. She says he’s right: that one’s hers. She has my flight home written on her hand. She read Matthew 2 because I said Sunday was Epiphany; Herod is a jealous showrunner. OFFICIALLY, in eyeliner, on a sign at the rope at Santa Barbara, in sunglasses at night. A girl from my flight filmed it, and by morning it was on a gossip blog. Skye put the still on her own Facebook herself. Her people wanted lunch: her mother, Debbie, who manages her, and her publicist, Corinne. The rules: no pictures, ‘a friend from school,’ February. Take the airport down. She took it down. There was a folder with my last name on it, and she pushed it back without opening it. At a gas station in Buellton she took the first picture of the two of us herself, at arm’s length, and put it up instead. Then she changed her status herself and made me say yes to it on her phone — the first thing anybody ever watched her do that nobody wrote. Monday she came to the Fishbowl and argued with me about a rose. My pie got her out of remedial math. Tuesday she taught me stick in an empty lot — a voice for every stall. I do a bad Frank. We argued Conan. She posted a picture of me stalling. The radio, at 2:31: Haiti. At midnight she took the picture down — not for Corinne. Wednesday in the Brick she explained the plates under Haiti from her Oceanography book, read me Milton off the front of *Frankenstein*, and fell asleep on my shoulder. At the Haiti table she borrowed Becca’s apron and was Cassidy for twenty dollars a name, and asked me where God was at 4:53. Met Laney. Met everybody. Corinne wanted a statement; she told her the girl at the table was right about the pictures, and hung up. That night she asked me to say one for them, from her. ‘Saturday.’ Thursday Margot interviewed her at the Anchor; she says I’m the same in every room. Saturday at dawn she taught me again, inside the Point. Still very bad at it. She posted it and kept it up. She came to Sully’s and learned the Who Dat. Laney took a shot at her; she had it handled, she says, and I didn’t let her finish, and she says she’ll reward that sort of behavior. In the Saab I told her some about Lena — that we were close in the fall. She said she can tell there’s a rest. She drove me to confession, and went back to Sully’s without me. Saturday night she read me Sunday’s Gospel off her phone. Three nights in LA: a fitting for the wedding episode — she’s not the bride, she checked. Tuesday she made me explain Massachusetts while I walked. The tornado took Sol’s swing. Wednesday she drove home with the top down in the rain and put the two of us up on Facebook, soaked. Thursday we argued the Supreme Court under one umbrella until it turned inside out. She’s been a corporation since she was twelve — Skylark Pictures; her mother named it. She wrote my brother, in capitals; Rudy says write the number big. Friday the sun came out, and she called the telethon as Skylark. Saturday she drove six hours to the Walk for Life, walked the whole thing arguing with me, and stood in front of Clare when a man started screaming. Sunday she came to Mass. I told her why I didn’t go up. Out past the break I told her what I know about the basement, which isn’t much, and about Nonna’s question and Danny’s. She’s the answer to both. She knows there’s more; she said that’s enough. She asked me to teach her Nonna’s prayer. Monday a blog found the back of my head; Gina knew Danny’s jacket before the commenters did. Corinne called her at six: every picture of us down until there’s a strategy. At noon in her room I was the one who didn’t want to stop, and she stopped it — for Sunday. She’d read up on confession to do it: I can’t walk in on Wednesday with a plan, and she won’t be my plan. Ask her again after she’s watched me go up. She asked me what I lose when I sit in the pew, and I told her: they pass the plate over you. She watched them do it on Sunday and didn’t know what she was watching. Then she took a picture of us without looking, and that night she put it up, captioned with Corinne’s own rule — *my friend from school.* At the lunch in Studio City her shoes stayed on. When they got to Danny she came back for that and nothing else, and said his number from memory. In the car she said she’s very good at fine. She heard me tell Ma *tomorrow*, and that I think she’s the answer, and took the picture down at the Las Posas exit without a word. Sol’s swing is up. I told her I don’t care, and she could tell. She’s stopping anyway. She wants Nonna to like her. Wednesday she said Theo and Laney were running lines. Wednesday night she was at the curb when I got home from confession. She asked if I went. Then, in the middle of a bit about a Supreme Court justice, I said it first. I didn’t know I was going to. She’d been carrying it since Monday, and she was going to say it first. She said it back. Thursday she took me to a fundraiser in the Palisades and never said what for — it didn’t occur to her anybody would mind. It was for Boxer: Corinne wanted me in the picture so the march would stop being a story. She saw my face across the room and asked twice. I told her it was fine — she came to my Walk and took the other side seriously, so I could stand in hers. So she went back in and got the whole room to argue with me, the real arguments, in Gil’s living room, for two hours, and made sure every one of them knew where I stand. We stayed till the end. At a taquería at the bottom of Sunset she wouldn’t post Corinne’s picture. She blew me a raspberry and posted one of us at the table instead: we agree on each other, and we’re not just friends from school. She’s a union member. Two of them. Her father was Pat Doyle, a juicer on the Meridian lots, gone since she was four. Then she said her name. Mary Catherine Callender-Doyle. Baptized at St. Mary’s in Lancaster, named for his mother. The only name she has that her mother didn’t give her. I sent the first two to Gina for Nonna. At three in the morning I made the picture my profile picture. She says I stole her art. She says happy looks good on me. Friday she argued Margot to a draw and went home to learn lines. Saturday at the Point I told her Nonna lit a candle for Maria Caterina. Saturday night on the bluff she kept her word: tomorrow. Sunday she sat in the same pew, in a cardigan she bought for Mass, and watched me go up, and knelt. That night she asked first, before anything. I told her it’s still no, for now. And that it’s closer than it’s ever been. She asked what question she’s the answer to. I told her Nonna asked me what makes me pray. She asked if she does. Yes. She wants to be the good thing, with the lights off. I stayed. Just sleep. Monday she picked Danny’s birthday book on State Street — O’Connor, all the stories — and wrote the card herself, in capitals. She says Gretta’s the only one at that party who isn’t acting. At a red light the radio played it, the day before his birthday, and we sang it at each other with the top down. Somebody filmed it. Tuesday her people were on the phone by six. She didn’t share it; she wrote on my wall instead: bring the clean version next time. I told her I was sorry about her job. She kissed me on the Morro steps in front of everybody and told me never to apologize for making her happy. Then Danny called on his birthday and she got on the phone. She told him I tricked her. Then she told him the truth: she was about to leave when I walked over, and she still has the book, with CON crossed out. Candlemas she held my candle while I knelt. That night she came up to my room for the first time. She didn’t ask. When she asks again, she says, she wants me to have nowhere to be in the morning. She asked if there’s a version of later she’s in. Wednesday on the swing, coats on, she kept me in the daylight. She’s in Vancouver for two weeks, a pilot, from Friday. She told me to go to New Orleans and watch my Saints win. Maybe it’ll be good for you guys, she said. I said yes. Thursday we skipped the rest of the day for the Point. Sol let her into the darkroom in January, for the project. Thursday night it was full of me — asleep, the back of me on the Point, the two of us on the swing — pictures I didn’t know anybody was taking. She gave me the swing: NOT FOR POSTING. It’s in Hale’s book. She propped the door open on purpose. She asked. She was the one who said no. Her father called her Mary Kate. He left in the dark for a five o’clock call when she was four, kissed her, told her to go back to sleep, and didn’t come back. Everybody she’s ever loved had a call time. When I come back she wants the truth, to her face. I promised. She drove me up the hill at three and waited in the Saab under the bell tower with three suitcases in the back. Friday at a quarter to five she stood with us in the lot while Osei blessed the van, with her eyes shut, and looked at the water on the back of her hand. Bye, Coat check. She went north. We went south. Friday at a truck stop under Picacho Peak she called from Burnaby. Wardrobe took my flannel: Cassie wears it; it got the part. The geese are the size of Labradors. I read her one of Hale’s rude ones at the pump. Saturday night she called again after wrap, and I read her two more, on the Broussards’ front steps. I told Lena’s little sister who she is. My girlfriend. In Canada. She wants a call at the kickoff. Sunday at the kickoff I had the phone open to call her, and it rang in my hand. She was in a trailer in Burnaby in a Colts cap, wearing it into Cassie’s wig. She bought her own *Moviegoer* at the airport and read it on the plane. Being in the movie doesn’t make anything real either, she says. She owes me a picture. She turned her TV off to hear the kickoff on Dupre Street. Her text after the game got to me at a quarter to four in the morning, on Esplanade. She’s taking full credit. Monday she called at her lunch from Burnaby: she cried for real in the Wade scene and the director kept it. Nobody can tell, she says. That’s the problem with being good. Wednesday the torch went past craft services. Tonight’s the moon.

choices.key: On the Broussards’ front steps Skye called at her lunch. Tonight’s the moon. You told her you love her.
response: “Love you,” he says. “Go be the moon.”
“Love you. Go be the front steps.” The door on her end opens on the lot and the noise comes back in. “Bye, Mid-City.”
Behind him the chain of the swing creaks once against its hook, and stops.
He shuts the phone on his knee.

choices.text: “Tell the torch I said who dat.”

response: “Tell the torch I said who dat.”
“I’ll tell him. He’ll be insufferable. He already thinks he’s the point of the Olympics.” Her door opens on the lot and her name comes in with the noise. “Bye, Mid-City.”
He shuts the phone on his knee with her laugh still in it.

choices.key: On the Broussards’ front steps Skye called at her lunch. Tonight’s the moon. You told her you miss her, and you’ll be here.
response: “I miss you,” he says. “I’ll be here.”

response.text: “I know where *here* is now,” Skye says. “It’s got a grandmother in it.” Her door opens on the lot. “Bye, Mid-City.”
response.else: “Here,” Skye says. “I’m holding you to *here*.” Her door opens on the lot. “Bye, Mid-City.”

response: He shuts the phone on his knee and keeps his hand on it.

s12a.slug: WEDNESDAY · 3:20 PM · DUPRE STREET, THE PORCH — UP THERE
body: The mail truck comes level with the house, and the carrier, a heavy man in a Saints toboggan with the USPS jacket over it, puts the Broussards’ mail in the box by the door and says “Who dat” to Jack for good afternoon. Jack says it back. The truck goes on down Dupre Street toward the bayou.
From the swing, behind him, Lena says, “Is she all right? Up there?”
He turns round on the step. She has the keys in her lap and her eyes on him, and the carnations in their newspaper beside her.
“She’s working all night.”
Lena takes her boots down off the rail, one and then the other, and the swing goes back under her and comes forward and she lets it. “Then she’s all right.”

She stands up off the swing with the keys in one hand and the carnations in the other. Up close the carnations smell faintly of cloves, and of wet stems and newsprint, and somebody has written the price on the paper in ballpoint, a dollar fifty. She puts them in his hands, stems first.
“Come on,” she says, and starts down the steep steps ahead of him.

s13.slug: WEDNESDAY · 3:45 PM · ST. LOUIS CEMETERY NO. 3, ESPLANADE AVENUE — THE GUIDRY TOMB
body: The sun has already gone low enough to get in under the oaks, and it lies along the Esplanade neutral ground in long bars, yellow and no warmer for it. They walk up the avenue toward the bayou on the side with the old houses, Lena with her hands in the pockets of her jean jacket and the strand from Laney still doubled round her wrist, Jack carrying the carnations like he was sent to the store for them. They pass Holy Rosary. Father Hébert’s car is in the lot behind the church with a black-and-gold flag on its antenna. She doesn’t slow down.

The cemetery is the next block, almost at the water: a long white wall along the avenue and an iron gate standing open in it, and inside the gate a man in a cap on a folding chair with a ring of keys on his knee and a radio going low, who looks at the carnations and nods them in.

Inside it’s a town. The tombs stand shoulder to shoulder down narrow lanes with names on the corners, little houses for the dead with peaked roofs and iron fences and doors of marble, some no bigger than a toolshed and some like chapels, and most of them white. Urns. Plaster saints with their noses gone. A few have split along a seam and been patched with brick and left that way. In Youngstown you put people in the ground, out at Calvary under the snow, and every spring the frost heaves the stones a little crooked, and somebody goes out with a level. Here they keep them up in the air, in houses, on streets. On ground this low, that makes a kind of sense.
Lena knows the way without looking at the corners. Left, and left again, and halfway down a lane where the light comes in low between the rows, she stops.

It’s not one of the big ones. Two vaults, one over the other, a peaked roof with a small cross on it, GUIDRY cut over the door, and the marble tablets on the front with the names going down them, the oldest worn soft and the newest cut sharp. It’s white as a Sunday shirt, fresh, the whitewash still clean down into the corners and over the cracks.
“Wes did that,” she says. “Every All Saints since the storm. He did it this year too.” She touches the corner of the tomb with her knuckles. “Mémère asked him about the ring right here.”
Jack says nothing.

She takes the carnations out of his hands and lays them on the ledge under the names, newspaper and all, and works Laney’s gold strand off her wrist and lays it across them. She puts her hands back in her jacket. She tells her grandmother the score.

“Grandmère. *Trente et un, dix-sept.*” She says it to the newest name, part French, part English, the way her father reads the sports page at the table, and she doesn’t skip. “Brees, thirty-two of thirty-nine. Hartley three field goals, and every one of them people said he couldn’t. Porter took it back seventy-four yards the other way, and I know, I know, you don’t care, you never cared, I’m *telling* you anyway. *Écoute.*”
“Tell her about the onside kick.”

“I’m *getting* to the onside kick.” She doesn’t turn round. “Start of the second half, Grandmère. We kicked it short, on purpose, in the Super Bowl, and we got it back, and the house went up so loud Aints went under the table and wouldn’t come out till the fourth quarter.”
She stops, and wipes under her nose with the back of her wrist.
“She hated it,” she says, to Jack. “Football. All of it. She’d have been on the porch with Daddy and a rosary, saying it was a sin to want anything that much.”
“Was it?”
“She’d have been inside by the third quarter. Watching through the screen door.” She looks at the name. “Saying the rosary *for* them.”
A mockingbird is going on top of a tomb two lanes over, running through everything it knows. The low sun has got onto the GUIDRY tablet and the letters stand up out of it in shadow.

“She sewed,” Lena says. “For money, for people Uptown, hems and wedding dresses, in her front room with the pins in her mouth. She talked through them. She could tell you all about yourself with a mouthful of pins and you’d understand every word. She made the christening gown, the one we all wore. Luc first, in 1985. Then all of us. Lucille in January, and Lucille screamed through the entire Rite like she knew whose it was.” She smiles at the tablet. “She let me run the treadle on the old Singer when I was six. I sewed her apron to Mrs. Lacoste’s tablecloth. She wore it home like that, the apron and the tablecloth, to show Mama what I did.”
He laughs at that, and she looks at the tablet as though her grandmother had.

“She called me Magdalena. The whole name. Every time, even yelling.” She counts them off on the fingers of the hand at her side, not looking at them. “Grandmère. Mémère, when I’m in trouble. Father Hébert, because he poured the water.”

body.text: “Professor Hale, once, and I fixed that.”

body: “— and —”

She stops. Her hand hangs at her side with the names folded down into it and the next finger still up. She reaches down with the other one and turns a carnation on the ledge so its head faces the name.
The mockingbird does all the talking.
“I’ve never asked Mama one thing,” Lena says. “You know that.”
“I know.”
She nods, at the tomb. Out on Esplanade a bus pulls away from the stop with a long hiss of brakes.

She unbuttons the breast pocket of her jean jacket and takes out the medal. It rode home from Canal in there with the flap buttoned down over it, and the chain comes out after it in a little gold heap in her palm, the oval face of it turned up: Our Lady with her hands open and the rays coming off them, and the words round the edge. She tries the clasp. The ring at the end of the chain has sprung open in the crowd, and her fingers are red and stupid with cold, and she gets it in her nails and loses it, and gets it, and loses it again.
“Do it for me.”
She holds it out to him. She turns her back on him and on her grandmother’s name, and puts her other hand up and gathers her hair off her neck and holds it in a twist on top of her head.

He has the chain in his fingers. His hands are no better than hers, in this, but they were raised on Glenwood Avenue, on furnace filters and the pull chain of a garage door that came apart every winter, and he knows this ring. He gets it between his thumb and the side of his first finger and closes the gap with his thumbnail, a hair at a time, till the ends meet. He brings the chain round her from behind, the medal down in front of her, and holds the two ends at the back of her neck.

The back of her neck is cold. There’s the small knob of bone at the top of her spine, and a few short dark hairs that never make it into the twist, and the collar of the sweatshirt, and his own knuckles against her skin. She smells of the market and her shampoo. He could put his mouth there. He knows exactly how far it is. He has the clasp in his fingers, and her grandmother’s name over her shoulder, and he doesn’t.

choices.text: *Fasten it, and leave your hands there a second.*
choices.key: At her grandmother’s tomb in St. Louis No. 3 the clasp of Lena’s medal was broken. Do it for me, she said. You fastened it, and left your hands there a second.
response: He hooks the clasp through the ring, and it holds, and he doesn’t take his hands away. They stay where they ended up, on her shoulders at the base of her neck, over the collar.

She lets him. Her hand comes down out of her hair, and her hair comes down over his wrists, all of it, cold on the outside and warm underneath, and her hand comes over his on her shoulder and covers it, and holds it there.

When she turns round, under his hand, the medal is where it lives. She touches it, and looks at the tomb. “She said this at every gate she ever went through. Church. Here. The Schwegmann’s lot.” And she says what’s written round the edge: “*O Mary, conceived without sin, pray for us who have recourse to thee.*”
He says it after her.
Down the lane the man in the cap is coming along the rows with his keys, rattling them to let the last of the living know. They go out the far side by the bayou, and he locks the gate behind them.

choices.key: At her grandmother’s tomb in St. Louis No. 3 the clasp of Lena’s medal was broken. Do it for me, she said. You fastened it and stepped back.
response: He hooks the clasp through the ring, and tests it once with a tug, and it holds. He takes his hands back and steps off a pace and puts them in the pockets of the Carhartt.

Her hair comes down. She turns round. Her hand goes up to the medal at her collarbone and stays on it a moment, her thumb on the face of it, and she looks at him over it with her eyes very steady, and then at the tomb.

“She said this at every gate she ever went through,” she says. “Church. Here. The Schwegmann’s lot.” And she says it, the words round the edge: “*O Mary, conceived without sin, pray for us who have recourse to thee.*”
He says it after her, from where he’s standing.
At the end of the lane the man in the cap has started along the rows with his ring of keys, shaking it at the tombs. They go out by the bayou side, and the gate goes shut on its chain behind them.

choices.key: At her grandmother’s tomb in St. Louis No. 3 the clasp of Lena’s medal was broken. You told her to hold still; she was shaking. It’s February in a cemetery, Jack.
response: Her shoulders are going under the sweatshirt, small and steady, and the chain jumps in his fingers with it.
“Hold still,” he says. “You’re shaking.”
“It’s cold.”
“It’s not that cold.”

“It’s February in a cemetery, Jack. It’s exactly that cold.” And she laughs, out loud, with her hair in her fist, loud enough that the mockingbird quits, and the laugh goes off down the lanes between the tombs, and he gets the clasp hooked while she’s still doing it.

She turns round with the medal where it lives, and puts her fingers on it, and is serious all at once. “She said this at every gate she ever went through. Church. Here. The Schwegmann’s lot.” And she says the words that run round the edge: “*O Mary, conceived without sin, pray for us who have recourse to thee.*”
He says it after her.
The man in the cap is coming down the lane with his keys, giving them a shake at every corner. They go out the bayou side, and he locks it after them.
